result:
I demonstrated orientation selectivity using DANDI:000021 (Allen Institute Visual Coding, Neuropixels), analyzing 1501 quality-passing units from six mice recorded simultaneously in thalamus (LGd) and six visual cortical areas while drifting and static gratings were shown. All NWB files were streamed with `remfile` range requests rather than downloaded.

**The core finding is that cortex encodes the grating's axis, not its direction of motion, and its thalamic input does not.** The clearest single-cell evidence is a VISp unit that fires strongly at 45° and 225° and is nearly silent at 135° and 315°: two lobes on one axis. Across the pooled population the median global OSI is 0.162 in cortex against 0.063 in LGd (Mann-Whitney p = 4.4 × 10⁻³¹), and 25–41% of cortical units per area meet a joint criterion of a per-unit shuffle test plus gOSI ≥ 0.25, against 5% of LGd units.

Four independent checks back this up. Preferred orientation estimated from disjoint halves of the trials agrees at circular r = 0.95 among selective units. It also survives changing stimulus family, agreeing between 2 s drifting gratings and 0.25 s static gratings at r = 0.86 with a median absolute offset of 5.4°. A leave-one-trial-out VISp population decoder gets the direction right on 68.4% of trials (chance 12.5%), but its errors are almost entirely the 180°-opposite direction (24% of trials, versus under 2% for each of the six other errors), so it recovers the correct axis on 92.1% of trials. Finally, a NeMoS Poisson GLM whose basis is periodic over 180°, and so cannot tell a direction from its opposite, predicts held-out VISp spike counts as well as a 360°-periodic model with twice the parameters (pseudo-R² ratio 0.99); in LGd that ratio drops to 0.85.

Two things worth flagging. First, the permutation test alone is a bad definition of "selective": 69% of LGd units clear p < 0.05 despite a median gOSI of 0.063, because the test detects any reproducible bias however small. That is why every headline fraction requires an effect-size threshold as well, and the README says so. Second, LGd was only recorded in two of the six sessions, so the thalamic comparison rests on 153 units from two mice.

Deliverables in the working directory are `orientation_selectivity.py` (jupytext), `orientation_selectivity.ipynb` (executed, no errors), ten `.png` figures, `orientation_selectivity_units.csv` with the per-unit results, `README.md`, and five supporting modules. One note: `01_load_data.py`, `02_probe_units.py`, and a 1.7 GB `lindi_cache/` were already in this directory from about three hours before my session started, apparently from an earlier LINDI-based attempt at the same dandiset. They are not mine and are unused by my pipeline, so I left them in place rather than deleting them.
